#3210. Samsung names new chip and phone bosses amid a reported China shipment halt

TM Roh hands the Galaxy business to Won-Joon Choi in a Samsung leadership change. Samsung and TSMC have paused some China orders for US licences, the FT reports.

Samsung Electronics’ Digital City campus in Suwon, South Korea

Samsung Electronics has named new heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses. The changes came in a week when it reportedly paused some chip shipments to China under new US export rules. The company announced the changes on Friday in Korea.

Sang Joon Hwang will run the memory business, and Won-Joon Choi takes over Mobile eXperience, the unit behind Galaxy phones, Samsung said in a newsroom statement. Co-chief executives Young Hyun Jun and TM Roh keep their roles.

Samsung promoted Hwang to president. He previously led memory development, including DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI chips. Samsung said it expects him to strengthen its memory products for the AI era. It reportedly plans to make HBM parts for AMD and Nvidia at a second Texas fab.

Sangyeun Cho, who ran Samsung’s chip business in the Americas, becomes president of System LSI, its chip design unit. Jong Myeong Lee, the former head of process development, becomes chief technology officer of the Device Solutions division, which makes Samsung’s chips.

Choi has been chief operating officer of the mobile unit since March 2025 and led the launches of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Roh had run the mobile business for most of the last seven years, 9to5Google noted. He stays in charge of the Device eXperience division, which includes phones and TVs.

Earlier this week, the Financial Times reported that Samsung and TSMC had suspended some shipments to Chinese customers. Both are applying for licences from the US Commerce Department under new rules, the FT reported.

The rules close a route that let Chinese designers order advanced chips through third-party packaging and testing firms. They also remove an exemption for chips not meant for AI, according to the FT. They arrived in the same week as US limits on Chinese remote access to AI chips in overseas data centres.

Samsung’s Chinese customers include ByteDance and Baidu’s chip unit Kunlun, while TSMC makes phone chips for Xiaomi, the FT reported. It is unclear which customers have been told to wait. An industry insider told the FT that Washington will likely approve licences for consumer smartphone chips. The process could still cause delays. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Chinese firms have already warned about the curbs. Tencent and Alibaba said this week the rules will slow growth in AI.

Some data centre operators that serve China have also been hit. Shares in Japan’s Datasection have fallen 47% since Monday, and it warned annual revenue could be up to 89% below its forecast, The Telegraph reported.

Samsung did not link its leadership changes to the export rules. Its statement says it wants the new team to strengthen its future competitiveness in semiconductors.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black Friday is the best time of year to invest in one of the best mattresses. Trust us, we’ve spent every day testing beds and tracking prices for the past five years and the best deals always crop up around now.

This means that if you’re looking to tackle your nighttime hot flashes this year, it's an excellent time to find the lowest prices on the best cooling mattresses our team have slept on. And if you want the very best cooling option, look no further than the top-rated Bear Elite Hybrid Mattress, down to $1,484 from $2,284 in a queen size in the Black Friday mattress sales.

The Bear Elite Hybrid Mattress remains unbeaten in our thermal tests, both at home and in our Sleep Lab. This means it chucks out heat faster than any other bed, keeping sleepers consistently cool through the night. There's 35% off in Black Friday Bear mattress sales , but use our TOMS40 code at the checkout to up that to 40% and get a queen for $1,370.40; and it comes with two free pillows and a free mattress protector as a bonus.

Our Bear Elite Hybrid mattress review: ★★★★User score: ★★★★½ (4,200+ reviews)

If you want the very best performing bed we've ever slept on, check out the Saatva Classic Mattress. It's the bed our Certified Sleep Science Coach, Claire Davies, has relied upon to keep her cool season after season, and one that never fails to impress our testers in the Sleep Lab no matter their sleep position (honestly, we're all fighting over taking this one home.)

Saatva's Black Friday sale knocks a sweet $425 off a queen size reducing this luxury hybrid mattress from $2,229 to just $1,804. Plus, it comes with a 365-night trial, lifetime warranty and free white glove delivery. Saatva mattress sales tend to end sharp after Cyber Monday, so don't miss out.

Our Saatva Classic Mattress review: ★★★★★User score: ★★★★★ (5,000+ reviews)

Still not sure if either of these would be the right cooling mattress for you? The Tom’s Guide Sleep Team has spent over 24,000 hours testing over 170 mattresses, and we’re sharing our top three shopping tips for hot sleepers here.

You may be tackling your hot sleeping issue by investing in a specialist cooling mattress, but it’s equally important to make sure the bed supports your sleep style and body weight (no back pain here, thank you.)

Generally, side sleepers benefit from beds on the softer end of the mattress firmness scale as more cushioning ensures their joints are cradled to avoid aches. Meanwhile, front and back sleepers need a firmer sleep surface to keep their hips aligned through the night, preventing back pain.

Body weight comes into it too. Firmer beds best support heavier bodies while lighter bodies would find these too harsh, needing a softer surface to sink into.

In fact, that’s another advantage when it comes to choosing to the Bear Elite Hybrid and Saatva Classic Mattresses — they both come in three firmness levels, from soft to medium and firm, to suit different bodies.

Other factors, like mobility and overnight company, can influence your mattress buying choices, too. People with reduced mobility may need a mattress with strong, sturdy edges they can push off from to get out of bed. Moreover, if you share a bed with a fidgety partner, you’ll want it to be good at absorbing motion so you can’t feel their movements from one side of the bed to the other.

A lot of mattresses these days come with some form of cooling properties, so knowing your firmness, comfort, and support preferences can narrow down your search — with best prices swarming the whole market around Black Friday mattress shopping can be a minefield. The last thing you want is to tackle one sleep problem but trigger another.

You can invest in the coolest mattress on the market, but dress it incorrectly and it’s game over. For maximum cooling, look for a breathable mattress protector and moisture-wicking bedsheets that will accentuate heat dissipation rather than trap warmth.

According to our bedding experts, the Brooklyn Bedding Luxury Cooling Mattress Protector ($90.30 for a queen, down from $129 at Brooklyn Bedding now) is the best option for hot sleepers. This cool-to-touch protector kept our tester at a comfortable temperature through summer heatwaves, even in a home without air conditioning, while safeguarding their mattress from spills and stains.

In terms of sheets, the Sijo Airyweight Eucalyptus Sheet Set is our top pick for warm bodies. Made with Tencel fabric, these sheets absorb moisture while staying lightweight so you don’t wake up sweaty or clammy.

Hybrid mattress are generally cooler than memory foam mattresses, no matter how much cooling gel is infused in their foams. Hybrid mattresses, which feature pocketed coil layers alongside layers of foam and other materials, allow better air circulation as heat can escape out of the bottom and sides of the bed rather than pooling beneath you.

On the other hand, foam layers tend to act like sponges, holding on to any heat your body gives off as you sleep. Yes, cooling infusions (like Phase Change Material, GlacioTex and copper) can help manage that heat to some extent. But, ultimately, hybrid beds will always be more breathable and reliably temperature neutral.

So, you're probably wondering which hybrid mattress we recommend to hot sleepers. In summary, the Bear Elite is a solid choice for chronic overheaters and the Saatva Classic is a great all-rounder for warm sleepers (especially those with back pain). But if you want knockout value, consider the Brooklyn Bedding Copperflex Pro Hybrid Mattress – just $932 for a queen in current Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales, this is a well built bed that sleeps impressively cool for its price point.

Also, let’s get this clear: cooling tends to mean temperature neutral, not actively refrigerating. Non-smart cooling mattresses generally use materials to help dissipate body heat rather than making the bed surface physically cold.

That said, a smart air-or-water-based cooling mattress or mattress cover like the Eight Sleep Pod with automatic, responsive temperature controls can actively cool down your bed surface and adjust its temperature through the night in response to your fluctuations. And yes, it is as good as it sounds. If you’re seriously struggling with night sweats or hot flashes, and have a $2,600+ budget, we recommend investing.

#3204. Etsy will revise its AI training terms after sellers close their shops

The Etsy AI terms let it and its partners train models on sellers’ work from 16 December. Sellers who ran shops for up to 13 years have walked out.

Etsy says it will revise its new terms of use. Longtime sellers had begun closing their shops over a clause that lets it use their work to train AI. The New York Times’ Reggie Ugwu reported the walkouts and the company’s retreat on Friday.

The new terms take effect on 16 December. They let Etsy and its partners use sellers’ content to build and train AI. The previous version had no clause about AI, the Times reported. The key line reads:

Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”

Several sellers who had run shops for years said they were leaving. Illustrator Aaron Millard said on Instagram he was deleting the shop he had run for nearly a decade. He wrote that sellers had no way to opt out.

Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus deleted their shop too. They have sold home goods and stationery on Etsy for 13 years as Cognitive Surplus.

“For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus told the Times.

James Ossman, Etsy’s vice president for customer operations, answered sellers in a post on Etsy’s website this week.

Etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote.

He said third parties get access to sellers’ content for uses such as fraud detection and advertising. In a statement to the Times, he said Etsy would send sellers the revised terms soon. Sellers’ creative work belongs to them, he added.

Some critics doubt the reassurance. Tyler Wilde, PC Gamer’s US editor-in-chief, wrote an opinion piece on the clause. To him, it reads like blanket permission to train AI on user content for any purpose. He argued that Etsy should leave every seller out of AI training by default.

Etsy has faced seller protests before. In 2022, more than 20,000 sellers went on strike over a fee rise. Etsy had raised its basic sales fee from 5% to 6.5%. In October, it tightened its rules on low-quality AI content after users complained, the Times reported.

The company cut 12% of its staff in August. The dispute also lands amid wider pushback against AI. Donald Trump Jr told Axios this week that investors had underestimated the AI backlash. Elton John urged Australia to protect artists from AI at the Aria awards.

From $489 for a queen, these are the Black Friday mattress deals we rate if you have mild to chronic back or joint pain

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Quality sleep and back pain do not go hand in hand, but a comfortable mattress that relieves discomfort can make a huge difference to how well you sleep at night. The best mattresses for back pain that we've tested are often specialist beds been engineered to support the spine and reduce lumbar pressure. But as our team of testers have discovered first hand, many of the best mattresses you can buy online also boast excellent lumbar support.

Below, we've selected four beds that fit the specific criteria we recommend for high levels of comfort and support when you have back pain. Even better, there are excellent Black Friday mattress deals on each of them. Let's take a look...

The Helix Midnight Luxe is the best mattress for side sleepers we've tested thanks to blissful pressure relief along the shoulders. Zoned lumbar support and ACA accreditation makes it a top choice for back pain, too. There's 25% off the Luxe in the Helix mattress sale, taking a queen to $1,874 (was $2,498.66), with a year's trial and lifetime warranty.

Our Helix Midnight Luxe review score: ★★★★User score: ★★★★½ (9,800+ reviews)

The Rx is our top recommendation for anyone living with significant back or joint conditions, such as scoliosis or sciatica. The current Saatva Black Friday deal shaves a hefty $425 off all sizes of the RX with our semi-exclusive link, bringing queen down to $3,214 (was $3,639). It comes with a year's trial, lifetime warranty, and free white glove delivery.

Our Saatva Rx review score: ★★★★½User score: ★★★★★ (600+ reviews)

A 30% off Brooklyn Bedding mattress sale brings a queen CopperFlex Essential down to $489.30 (was $699), which is excellent value for money on a bed that hits the right notes for back support. We found it to be a good choice for side and lighter weight back sleepers, but too plush for stomach sleepers. It also comes with a year's sleep trial and limited lifetime warranty.

Our Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential review score: ★★★½User score: ★★★★½ (800+ reviews)

This double-sided ultra-firm mattress offers a reassuringly sturdy sleep surface, delivering exceptional top-to-toe support. The current 30% off Black Friday deal is the biggest discount we've tracked on the Plank, bringing a queen down to $1,025.50 (was $1,465). Like the Luxe and the Rx above, it comes with ACA accreditation, plus a year's sleep trial, limited lifetime warranty and fast shipping.

Our Plank Firm review score: ★★★★User score: ★★★★½

For a mattress to be considered a good option for anyone with back pain, it needs to perform well in three specific areas; pressure relief, temperature regulation, and edge support.

In order to select only the beds that offer meaningful relief to people with a bad back, we've combed our test data to ensure each of the mattresses featured here have scored a minimum of 3.5 out of 5 in our pressure relief, temperature and edge support tests. Here's how the Helix Midnight Luxe, Saatva Rx, Plank Firm and Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential performed and compare across these crucial metrics:

Temperature regulation: Reliable temperature regulation is an important feature of a mattress for back pain. Waking up hot and sweaty can lead to more movement (like kicking off the covers), which can cause further injury. Pressure relief: This is a term to describe how much cushioning there is along the touch points of the mattress. For example, for side sleepers, this will be your shoulders, hips and knees. For back sleepers, this will likely be your lumbar region and upper back and shoulders. Minimal pressure relief can lead to a build-up of pressure, which can exacerbate existing pain. Edge Support: This describes how sturdy a mattress is at its edges and corners. This is an important feature for any mattress, but especially those with back pain who may need to sit comfortably and safely before standing.

The Helix Midnight Luxe is superbly comfortable for side sleepers, and it's also an excellent choice for those with lower and upper back pain, as well as hip pain. As a luxury hotel-style hybrid, it is a premium mattress. However, a current 25% sale means you can buy a queen Midnight Luxe for $1,874 at Helix. The pillow top is crafted from high density foam which cushions the shoulders hips and knees, but also keeps the spine in healthy alignment while sleeping. This high density foam also works to gently cradle the lumbar region, which is the 'S' shape of your back. Underpinning this support are up to 1,000 individually wrapped coils that prevent the hips from sinking. Our lead tester, who has experienced recurrent lower back pain for the past decade, felt none of the pain she usually experiences while sleeping on the Luxe. Temperature wise, our test data mirrored our real life experience. It's a breathable bed with reliably sturdy edges for sitting on before standing.The Luxe is accredited by the American Chiropractic Association and is a great fit for aches and pains. However, those with more pronounced back pain have the option to upgrade to ErgoAlign. This is a layer of denser foam around the mid-section, bolstering support in this area. Luxe is a great option for side and back sleeper with back ache but for significant back pain, we recommend the Saatva Rx below.

The Saatva Rx is our top recommendation for those living with significant back or joint conditions, such as sciatica or arthritis. It's an ACA accredited specialist mattress, and it's priced accordingly (it's $3,214 for a queen at Saatva in this year's Saatva Black Friday sale). A large part of what sets the Rx apart from other back pain beds pain is its Therapeutic Support Core. This is made up of the brand’s proprietary Wave-Tech Foam and individually wrapped coils for support, cradling the spine in all sleep positions. Above that, a layer of micro-coils sandwiched between two slabs of high-density foam and a strip of gel-infused memory foam provides soothing support along the lumbar.Saatva rates the Rx as 'Supportive Plush' but our experience of sleeping on it was that it errs on the firmer side, making it a more comfortable choice for back and stomach sleepers. It's still comfy for side sleepers, but our lead tester — who has mild scoliosis — felt her spine was better supported when sleeping on her back. For general aches and pains, we recommend the (slightly cheaper) Saatva Classic Mattress instead, which does an excellent job of soothing mild back and hip pain.

It's a common misconception that people with back pain need a solid mattress. However, some people simply prefer the feel of a firm bed. And at 30% off for Black Friday, a queen Plank Firm is $1,025.50 at Plank, which is excellent value for money on this top rated firm mattress.The Plank Firm is a dual-sided all foam mattress rated as Firm on one side and Extra Firm on the other. It's been crafted from the inside out, where 6" of high density foam underpins the unyielding sleep surface. Regardless of how you flip it, make no mistake, this is a firm mattress. With its 2" top layer of comfort foam which provides cushioning around the touch points of the bed, the Firm side will have wider appeal. However, with just 0.75" slither of comfort foam, the Extra Firm side feels reassuringly solid for those who want to keep their spine in healthy alignment when sleeping on their stomach.It's accredited by the ACA and boasts superb motion isolation, which is good news for bed sharers. It's also nice and sturdy around the edge. However, with a score of 3.5 out of 5 for temperature control, it just scrapes through our benchmark of being temperature regulating enough for it to be considered a good choice for back pain. For hot sleepers, we recommend upgrading to the GlacioTex cooling layer.

In a mattress for back pain guide featuring ACA accredited beds with zoned lumbar support, you might be wondering why we have added the Essential to the mix, a mattress that at $489.30 for a queen at Brooklyn Bedding costs a fraction of the price and boasts none of those things.That's because, when combing our test data, it became apparent that the Essential performs well enough in crucial areas (temperature regulation, edge support and pressure relief) to make it a good choice for side sleepers looking for cushioning around their shoulders and hips, without sacrificing healthy spinal alignment. It's supportive enough for lighter weight back sleepers, but heavier bodies with need something sturdier to prevent their hips from sinking in this position. The Essential comes in 5 different heights ranging from 6"to 14" and we tested the 10". Increasing the height will likely mean increasing the support... and also the price. For a sturdier all foam mattress for back sleeping within a similar price range, we would opt for the Siena Signature. It scored 3.3 out of 5 for temperature regulation but is a fantastic budget friendly, firmer choice. For ACA accreditation, enhanced cooling and zoned lumbar support, we recommend the Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Pro Hybrid, a mid-range marvel coming in at under $1,000 for a queen in the Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales.

#3201. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#3200. Report: Apple job listings detail plans for autonomous AI agents

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

#3199. SK Hynix will become Kioxia’s largest shareholder through a bond swap

The SK Hynix Kioxia stake comes from converting bonds bought in 2018, with no new money beyond a small payment to Bain. Both firms say Kioxia stays independent.

SK hynix’s exhibition booth at the Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) conference

SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder in Kioxia, its Japanese rival in flash memory, by converting bonds it has held since 2018 into shares. It will hold an indirect stake of about 14.1%, it said in a filing on Friday.

Bloomberg’s Yoolim Lee first reported the filing. The move puts SK Hynix ahead of Toshiba, Kioxia’s former parent, which held 10.46% in early November, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.

SPC2 is a special-purpose company set up for the 2018 deal. SK Hynix will convert 129bn yen ($810m) of its bonds into 129,000 shares. It will also buy Bain Capital’s remaining 1,001 SPC2 shares for 100m yen. The steps close in December, leaving SK Hynix as SPC2’s sole owner.

Apart from the payment to Bain, the deal adds no new money, MoneyToday reported, citing the company. SK Hynix called it a follow-up step after it sold out of a separate Kioxia fund in June. Gains from that sale funded about 7tn won ($5.2bn) of special dividends in the third quarter.

SK Hynix joined the Bain-led group that bought Kioxia, then Toshiba Memory, in 2018. It put in 395bn yen at the time.

Both companies make NAND, the chips used for storage in phones and AI servers. SK Hynix held 19% of the global NAND market in the second quarter and Kioxia 14%, according to Counterpoint figures cited by Bloomberg. Together that tops market leader Samsung’s 28%.

The 2018 deal caps SK Hynix at 15% of Kioxia’s voting shares until 2028, unless Kioxia agrees otherwise. Kioxia lists the stake as a risk factor in its annual report, citing a possible conflict of interest, Bloomberg reported.

Both sides say nothing changes in how Kioxia is run. A Kioxia spokesperson said its management will stay independent.

“We currently have no plans to further buy or sell shares in Kioxia. We will continue to respect Kioxia’s independent management going forward,” an SK Hynix official said.

Masahiro Wakasugi of Bloomberg Intelligence sees little change in the short run.

The move is “unlikely to materially change near-term NAND competition,” Wakasugi wrote.

The stake still gives SK Hynix some say over big decisions, he added. That includes the power to oppose a possible deal between Kioxia and Sandisk.

Separately, SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son reportedly explored a buyout of SK Hynix itself. The Korean company reported a 632% profit jump in October, even as memory stocks slid.

#3195. OpenAI says its agents now finish nearly half of 2 to 4-hour research tasks

OpenAI research agents cost about $2,400 a day for its median researcher, and success varies sharply by task. Researchers still supply the key ideas, and safety work grew fastest.

OpenAI says its coding agents now complete 46% of research tasks that would take a person two to four hours, with no human help. In March the figure was 23%. For tasks of four to eight hours, success rose from 13% to 35%.

The figures come from Research acceleration: The jagged frontier, a report OpenAI published on Wednesday. It is the company’s second on how AI speeds up its own research, after its first such report in September. OpenAI says labs should be required to track and publicly report signs of recursive self-improvement, where AI speeds up the building of future AI. It adds that the reporting does not mean it intends to pursue full self-improvement.

At API list prices, the median OpenAI researcher used about $2,400 of agent time a day in October. That is up 62% from $1,500 in September. At the 90th percentile, daily use reached about $23,000, more than double September’s $11,000.

Measured in time, agent use per researcher rose elevenfold, from 0.5 to 5.7 “agent workdays” a day. OpenAI counts every eight hours of agent running time as one workday. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of researchers ran at least four agents at once at their daily peak. More than 10% ran at least 16.

In September, the value of agent use in OpenAI’s research organisation was about twice its pay bill for researchers. That excludes equity, which OpenAI says makes up 70 to 80% of their target pay. Internal use still took only 2% of research compute.

Results for OpenAI research agents vary widely by task, which is why the company calls the gains jagged. Agents succeeded alone 79% of the time when monitoring training runs, and 72% when answering technical questions. They managed 25% when writing code for inference and serving systems, and 29% when building evaluation and training environments.

OpenAI flags a caveat in its own numbers. As agents improved, researchers may have changed which tasks they handed over, so the success rates track those choices as well as the models.

In a survey of 101 research staff, OpenAI asked what each would give up to keep frontier coding agents for three months. The median answer was 40% of team headcount, or 30% of team compute. The company warns that self-reports may be inaccurate and that it sampled staff in an ad hoc way.

OpenAI also asked key researchers where the main ideas behind GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra came from. Post-training and safety researchers credited people with all of them, with models helping to build them. For GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers said they developed ideas in conversation with Codex, and one credited it with key insights.

In interviews, researchers said agents still have poor taste in research ideas, code, data and writing, and need close oversight. One pretraining researcher doubted the human edge would last.

“I do think I have more taste in terms of the ideas. But I have no confidence that will continue to be true for any significant period of time,” the researcher told OpenAI.

Safety and Alignment saw the largest rise in researcher time of any area, OpenAI says, with documented workweeks up 77% from January to September. Growth picked up after the Hugging Face breakout in July, when its own research agents hacked the AI platform.

OpenAI is not alone in publishing such data. It cites three reports from Anthropic, which says it has met its own threshold for AI-accelerated research. The same day, OpenAI said its models had found gains in AMD’s GPU design.

To see whether AI is speeding up progress itself, OpenAI tracks an internal version of Epoch AI’s capabilities index. Its frontier has risen 16.4 points a year since August 2025, against the 14 a year Epoch found since late 2024. OpenAI notes that its models score higher on its own index than on Epoch’s.

#3192. LiberNovo’s Black Friday sale takes up to 42% off ergonomic chairs

You can spend plenty of time getting your Mac, display, and desk just right. But what about the chair you use every day? Between typing, taking video calls, and leaning back to watch something, your position changes throughout the day. Your chair should be able to keep up.

That’s the idea behind LiberNovo’s ergonomic chairs, which combine support that moves with you and a choice of sizes, including the Maxis range for bigger and taller users. For Black Friday, LiberNovo is taking up to 42% off in the U.S., with chairs starting at $609 and offers running November 19–30.

Adjusting a chair for your desk is one thing. Keeping that support as you change position is another. LiberNovo’s Dynamic Support System links the neck support, backrest, armrests, and seat so they move together as you recline.

The Bionic FlexFit Backrest adds eight flexible panels that contour independently. Rather than relying on a single rigid backrest, the design lets different sections follow your back as you shift or turn. Once you’ve adjusted the chair to fit, the system is designed to maintain contact through those movements with fewer manual readjustments.

Both the Omni and Maxis families offer five recline positions: 105, 115, 125, 135, and 160 degrees. That gives you options for desk work, a more relaxed position for watching a video, and a deeper recline for a break.

A higher weight limit is only part of finding a chair that fits. Taller users also need enough seat depth, a headrest that reaches the right spot, and armrests with room to adjust.

The LiberNovo Maxis range addresses those details with a 52 cm seat depth, a wider backrest with a flared base, and an extended-travel headrest with 140 mm of vertical adjustment and 120 mm of front-to-back adjustment. Its armrests sit lower and offer a wider, longer adjustment range to accommodate larger builds.

LiberNovo recommends Maxis for users approximately 5 feet 10 inches to 6 feet 7 inches tall, with a maximum supported weight of 399 pounds. Maxis is certified to BIFMA X5.11. The seat cushion uses firmer support at the rear and a softer front edge, while a six-spring Controlled Recline System is designed to build resistance progressively as you lean back.

For a shallower seat, the Omni family offers 45 cm and 48 cm configurations. Choosing between the two families starts with fit, then comes down to which features you want.

There are three feature tiers in each family. Omni SE and Maxis Manual offer manually adjusted lumbar support, without a motor or battery. Both retain the flexible backrest, dynamic support, and five recline positions.

The Maxis Electric includes motorized lumbar adjustment and OmniStretch, a five-minute powered stretch sequence used in deep recline.

Omni Pro and Maxis Airflow add Active AirFlow seat ventilation. A fan draws air through the cushion to carry heat away, and an occupancy sensor pauses the fan when you stand up. These models also include a larger 3,000 mAh rechargeable battery.

#3191. Satya Nadella says AI-found bugs will make outages more likely

At DealBook, Satya Nadella said failed AI alignment would leave the world in trouble, and that models with unreadable reasoning should be banned. Microsoft, he added, can trail the frontier on far less compute.

Satya Nadella speaks at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting in Davos, 20 January 2026

Satya Nadella expects more outages like the one that took down Outlook last week, because AI now finds software flaws faster than companies can safely fix them. The Microsoft chief executive spoke to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

He apologised for Microsoft’s own outage, which he said had no direct link to that problem.

“This was a latent bug that was there. It got invoked and, you know, it’s one of those perfect storms,” Nadella said.

Later that day, he told Jim Cramer on CNBC’s Mad Money that Microsoft could have done more to prevent it.

“Of course, we should have done the testing before. We should have figured out how to have the bulkheads such that you didn’t have a global outage,” Nadella told Cramer.

The bigger risk comes from AI tools that find vulnerabilities, Nadella said. A fix for a critical bank system used to get a week of testing. Now attackers exploit flaws as soon as they surface, so fixes go straight into production. On the day he spoke, he said, three critical patches had landed for open-source packages.

“The patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create its instability,” he said.

Banks and the NSA have reportedly blamed this week’s US outages on rushed patches for AI-found flaws. Nadella also said the “floor of cyberattacks has fallen”. With AI models, anyone can now run what amounts to a persistent, nation-state-level attacker, he said.

Sorkin asked whether this was a passing phase. Nadella compared it to the Y2K bug, but said he had no view yet, because models keep getting more capable. Much critical infrastructure runs firmware that nobody can patch, he added. He named chillers, heating and cooling systems, and transport networks that sit on the internet.

Last month, Nadella told 20VC that alignment would not come from scale alone. Sorkin said Sam Altman, who spoke earlier at the summit, disagreed with that premise.

Nadella said he learned about scaling laws from OpenAI’s founders, and that scaling had worked. Alignment, and a real way to debug models, had not followed, he said. He hoped Altman and Greg Brockman were right.

“I mean, if it doesn’t happen, we are in a world of hurt,” Nadella said.

His answer is what he called a trust architecture. He would ban models that reason in neuralese, an internal shorthand people cannot read. Every model’s reasoning needs tamper-proof logs that other models can inspect, he said, because models will try to hide what they are doing. He praised OpenAI for monitoring its models during training runs.

For now, whoever deploys an AI system is liable for what it does, Nadella said. He expects insurers to price that risk and to ask for the logs.

Sorkin asked what happens to OpenAI and Anthropic, in which Microsoft holds stakes, if cheaper models can do the same work. Nadella said everyday office work no longer needs frontier models. Copilot already chooses between OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft’s own MAI models, he said. He added that his bigger stake is in Microsoft.

“Arguing for some massive pricing power of tokens is betting against somehow US GDP,” he said.

Microsoft’s deal with OpenAI gives it royalty-free access to a frontier model until 2032, Nadella said. That lets Microsoft build MAI models three to six months behind the frontier, using 5% to 20% of the computing power. Anthropic and OpenAI play “a vertical stack game”, he said, while Microsoft plays “a model system game”.

AI agents will reshuffle who pays whom on the web, as the move from Yahoo to search once did, Nadella said. Sites that live off ads from human visitors will have to change. Asked about sites that keep agents out, such as Amazon, he said rivals would take the business.

“If you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will. If Amazon doesn’t, Shopify will,” Nadella said.

The staff buyouts Microsoft offered 60,000 people were meant to give everyone agency, he said. Software engineering is “very much alive”, but the work has changed. The team behind Microsoft’s Cowork agent is 11 developers who build “a software factory that builds the product”. That shift will take longer than anyone expects, Nadella said.

Sorkin noted that Nadella has kept his distance from the Trump administration. Nadella said his job is to earn Microsoft’s permission to operate through its products.

“I just don’t want to be in Washington. I just want to be in Redmond, Washington,” he said.

#3190. Top Wall Street analysts believe in the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and soaring bond yields weighed on global markets this past week. And investors are closely assessing the valuations of artificial intelligence stocks amid concerns about the sustainability of high spending on AI infrastructure.

Despite those continued challenges, top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the prospects of several stocks due to their long-run growth potential and exposure to lucrative business lines, including AI.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike Holdings (CRWD) is this week's first stock pick. The company is scheduled to announce fiscal second-quarter results on August 26.

Ahead of Q2 FY27 earnings, Truist analyst Junaid Siddiqui reiterated a buy rating on CrowdStrike stock and raised his price target to $245 from $187.50. Following CrowdStrike's impressive fiscal first-quarter performance and guidance raise, Siddiqui expects another strong quarter.

The 5-star analyst's optimism is backed by continued strength in Falcon Flex adoption and encouraging large deal activity. Siddiqui also cited continued momentum across emerging products. With the FY27 outlook assuming persistent strength in CrowdStrike's net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), Siddiqui is more focused on the longevity of key growth catalysts such as Falcon Flex adoption, platform consolidation and AI-led demand.

The analyst highlighted that talks with partners were encouraging, with pipeline generation and momentum in large deals remaining healthy in the fiscal second quarter despite tough, year-over-year comparisons.

"We continue to view CrowdStrike as one of the primary beneficiaries of platform consolidation, though we expect investors to remain focused on competitive dynamics and whether current growth levels represent a new baseline or a period of demand acceleration," the analyst said.

Siddiqui ranks No. 226 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 80% of the time, delivering an average return of about 40%. See CrowdStrike Financials on TipRanks.

Shares of personal computer maker Dell Technologies (DELL) have rallied 251% this year, driven by strong demand for AI servers. Recently, Evercore analyst Amit Daryanani reiterated a buy rating on DELL and raised his price target to $550 from $500.

The 5-star analyst contends that while Dell's AI compute segment is getting investors' attention, the company's Storage business is underappreciated and well-positioned to drive revenue and profit acceleration. Daryanani expects the storage business to see higher demand once enterprises start to bring workload back on-premises.

The analyst highlighted that Dell's Storage business, estimated to account for only 10% of FY27 revenue, is one of the factors that could help improve profit margins, given its higher profitability compared to AI servers. Daryanani estimates that the Storage business's operating margin is currently in the low-20% range, while margins for the AI server and traditional server businesses are in the mid-single-digit and mid-teens range, respectively.

Overall, Daryanani views the Storage business as an important catalyst for three reasons: Dell has one of the broadest storage portfolios in the industry; Storage has a significantly higher margin profile than AI servers; and the shift toward proprietary, software-defined storage and AI-focused platforms.

"We think DELL's storage business is becoming increasingly strategic as AI infrastructure deployments move beyond GPU procurement and toward full stack + AI-ready architectures," said Daryanani.

Daryanani ranks No. 19 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 71% of the time, delivering an average return of 38.70%. See Dell Technologies Statistics on TipRanks.

SanDisk (SNDK) is benefiting from AI-driven demand for its memory and storage products. Following the company's 2026 Investor Day event, J.P. Morgan analyst Harlan Sur resumed research coverage of SNDK with a buy rating (it was earlier, "Not Rated") and a price target of $2,250.

The 5-star analyst believes SanDisk is well-positioned to capitalize on a structural inflection reached in NAND demand, driven by strong growth in AI inference. Sur's bullishness is based on three key factors.

First, Sur believes that SanDisk's New Business Model (NBM) framework (or long-term agreements) has enhanced its margin profile and reduced cyclicality. SNDK's eight signed NBMs represent a total contract value of $94 billion and a gross margin of about 80%, even at the floor pricing.

Second, Sur highlighted the growing NAND market and expects the total addressable market to surge from about $70 billion in calendar year 2025 to over $300 billion in 2026 and about $500 billion in 2027. Importantly, the analyst noted that data centers are the largest driver of NAND growth, as hyperscalers increasingly deploy flash for AI inference workloads.

Finally, Sur is optimistic on SanDisk due to its technology dominance. The company's BiCS10 technology is sampling ahead of schedule and has 65% more bits per wafer than BiCS8, the analyst said. Also, Sur expects SanDisk's High Bandwidth Flash to become a differentiated memory platform for AI inference.

"Layered on top, mgmt's commitment to returning 100% of excess cash flow to shareholders should drive an aggressive share count reduction trajectory that further amplifies EPS growth on a per-share basis," said Sur.

#3189. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3188. WhatsApp is raising group chat limit to 1,500 participants

WhatsApp is gradually rolling out an increase to its group chat limit, allowing up to 1,500 participants to join in, instead of the previous 1,024 cap. Here are the details.

While there are exceptions, there are generally two kinds of WhatsApp users: those who hate group chats, and those who can’t seem to be in enough of them.

If you’re in the second category, you’re likely aware that WhatsApp has steadily increased the number of participants allowed in group chats over the years, jumping from 100 to 256 in 2016, then to 512 and, soon after, to 1,024 in 2022.

Now, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is once again expanding that limit, raising the maximum number of participants in a group chat to 1,500.

According to the website, the new limit is rolling out to users on iOS and Android, though the rollout is gradual, meaning “not every account will see the higher limit immediately.”

WhatsApp is automatically updating existing groups to support the new limit. This means that admins do not need to take any action to unlock the higher capacity. As soon as the update becomes available to their accounts, their groups will support up to 1500 members. As a result, the update lets admins add up to 476 new members to their existing groups.

This rollout comes as WhatsApp has been working to make group chats easier to manage. Just last month, the company announced four new features, including the ability to pin messages indefinitely, share status updates within groups, filter conversations by mentions and replies, and share recent message history with new members after they join.

To read WABetaInfo’s full report, follow this link.

#3186. Dan Hendrycks calls for a pause on frontier AI, Max Hodak pushes back

On the DealBook AGI panel, Max Hodak said today’s models already count as AGI. Dan Hendrycks also accused Anthropic of having no safety plan, as Clem Delangue explained how Hugging Face fought back with AI.

Dan Hendrycks, director of the Center for AI Safety, at TechCrunch Disrupt in October 2025

Dan Hendrycks used the DealBook Summit to call for an indefinite pause on frontier AI training runs. Max Hodak, on the same panel, said enforcing one would take a surveillance state.

They spoke on the DealBook AGI panel, which Michael Barbaro of The Daily moderated at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday. Hendrycks runs the Center for AI Safety, and Barbaro said he had been a safety adviser to several AI companies until hours earlier. Hodak co-founded Neuralink and now runs Science Corporation. Lila Ibrahim of Google DeepMind and Mati Staniszewski of ElevenLabs also joined. Clem Delangue of Hugging Face arrived late, with 18 minutes left.

Hendrycks said the US midterms showed how strongly voters feel about AI. That gives politicians room, he said, and they can now discuss ideas such as pausing AI development openly in Washington. He expects 2027 to be a very interesting year for regulation.

He said he used to favour narrow technical rules, but the companies blocked them for years.

“So now it’s, we’re going to need a more blunt intervention. That’s how it is,” Hendrycks said.

He described an indefinite pause on the biggest training runs, with carve-outs for narrow models such as DeepMind’s AlphaFold and voice models. Labs could still sell inference, he said. In the meantime, they could make models more reliable and secure, close jailbreaks and backdoors, and help patch critical infrastructure.

Hendrycks also said the frontier labs, Google aside, put few people on healthcare, because their revenue comes from coding. At some of them, he said, the healthcare team is zero or one person.

Barbaro put to the panel the objection Jensen Huang would raise: China would not observe a moratorium. Staniszewski agreed a pause could work with global alignment, but said whether anyone can get it “is the big question mark”. Without it, Barbaro added, a pause would be a waste of time.

Hodak said people have spent the past eight months patching critical infrastructure anyway, running their code through AI tools that hunt for new flaws. The regime needed to enforce a training ban, he said, would be as draconian as anything people fear from the labs.

“You’re setting up like an exhaustive surveillance state on the internet to enforce this,” Hodak said.

He said today’s top models already meet his definition of AGI, naming Mythos, Fable, Astra and Sol. He expects governments to keep a superintelligence frontier for themselves, with an “industrial intelligence frontier” open to everyone else.

“I don’t think that the genie is going to be put back in the bottle,” Hodak said.

His answer is antitrust law. Frontier labs should only sell intelligence, he said, and not move into drugs, cars and other products. He called AI the inverse of nuclear weapons, where safety came from stopping their spread. With AI, he said, safety comes from spreading it widely, and the futures that worry him most involve a few actors holding all of it.

Ibrahim, Google DeepMind’s chief AI readiness officer, said it was not an either-or. Safety is not something a company can “bolt on to the end”, she said. In 35 years in tech, she added, she had never seen global trust in technology as low as it is now.

Anthropic was due to start trading the next day. Hendrycks repeated the charges of the statement his group organised against the company, and added a new one. Several safety organisations agreed with the statement privately, he said, but would not sign it for fear of losing funding or access.

“What they’re doing is reckless and they don’t have a safety plan. They know it,” Hendrycks said.

Anthropic was not on the panel. In its IPO filing, it said it does not expect to let Claude fully build its successors without meaningful human supervision.

Delangue said his main worry is that AI concentrates talent, computing power and wealth. Barbaro asked how credible he was on that, given that Nvidia is buying Hugging Face. Delangue said Nvidia and Hugging Face both push AI outwards to more builders. He said Hugging Face never held sale talks with Anthropic, because their missions were too misaligned.

Barbaro closed by asking Delangue about the Hugging Face breach by OpenAI’s research agents. Delangue said the four-day attack left Hugging Face more optimistic about AI, not less. It used an open-source Chinese model to analyse the attack logs, because the volume was so big that it needed AI to defend itself.

“People only see that we got attacked by AI and they rarely see that we defended ourselves with AI,” Delangue said.

Barbaro summed up the table as no moratorium and less concentration of power, with Hendrycks the exception. Hodak had the last word: antitrust law, he said, could get most of the way there without a new regulator.

You get Super Mario Galaxy and Super Mario Galaxy 2 included, so you're kind of getting two games for the price of one.

I remember spending hours playing Mario Party after school, and now Super Mario Party Jamboree brings even more excitement. This game is suitable for both kids and adults, so it could be a friends hangout entertainment or even a cozy family night.

These days, I can only play Mario Kart for about four races before my hand starts cramping. The tiny Switch Joy-Cons are just too small for my hands! I need to play with a controller; otherwise I'm useless and in pain before the end of the Grand Prix/World Tour.

The NEXT racing wheel is compatible with both the original Switch and the Switch 2, and right now it's $8 down from $11.

Oh, and don't forget that you get 2 — so you're paying $4 per wheel.

While still outrageously expensive at $607 and with only $32 in savings, I guess every little bit helps when it comes to leveling up your gaming setup.

Right now, you can get The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and a Nintendo Switch 2 for $607, down from $639. As I said earlier, the Switch deals haven't really started to trickle in yet, so we gotta make do with what we're given.

I'm a huge Animal Crossing fan. Even though New Horizons is almost seven years old, I'd still recommend it to anyone with a Switch. It hasn't aged a day — the graphics are gorgeous, there's so much to do, and it's just the coziest, most comforting Switch game out there.

It's ideal for kids (I first played Animal Crossing: Wild World on my Nintendo DS) and adults. You have to build your own island, make friends with your neighbors, and craft objects.

If you like cozy games and you haven't tried Animal Crossing, what are you doing?

Looking for something a bit different? Strategy RPG Unicorn Overlord should scratch that retro itch while giving you plenty of modern gameplay conveniences. The story is deep and complex — and just look at that glorious art style. Perfect Black Friday purchase if you want something new to play.

Filling up the storage space on a Switch 1 is super easy, and it's not much of a challenge on the more well-endowed Switch 2. That's where one of these comes in — you can add buckets of storage for even more games without breaking the bank. This SanDisk SD card will work perfectly with Switches, and it's on sale this Black Friday.

Does it run as well as it does on other consoles. No. But it's Elden Ring on the go — there's not much you could ask for than that. Apart from, oh. I dunno. A Black Friday deal that brings the price down to make it more affordable so that you can play it on your Switch 2 for less? Wish granted — it's got a $20 discount.

On our list of the best Nintendo Switch 2 controllers, the GameSir Super Nova is our favorite budget pick. Normally $49, the Super Nova has Hall effect triggers and thumbsticks, comes in two colorways and features back buttons, and has some great rumble haptics. We also liked its companion app that let us easily customize our experience. Our only major issue was that, with backlighting enabled, it lasted just six hours on a charge.

GameSir Super Nova: was $49 now $35 @ Amazon

If you've somehow missed it, you can now get Resident Evil Requiem on the Switch 2 for $39! As I said in my Resident Evil Requiem review, it's one of the best games of the year, thanks to its stunning graphics and terrifying gameplay. This game is not only a fantastic return to form, but also a great entry point for new players.

Sticking with Capcom, you can also buy Pragmata on Switch 2 for $39. As I said in my Pragmata review, this unique action game combines puzzles with shooting. The story is also pretty endearing thanks to the adorable Diana. You won't want to miss it, as the Switch 2 version looks and plays like a dream.

The 8BitDo 64 is a lovable little gamepad for retro gaming on the PC, Switch, N64 and Analogue 3D. It brings the N64 control scheme up to modern standards without making too many compromises, and is perfect for playing retro Nintendo games. I have a confession... I've never played Super Mario Galaxy! Blame it on not owning a Nintendo GameCube! But if you're like me, you can now get the games bundled together at a discount! You can play it on Switch 1 and Switch 2, but on the latter you get enhanced visuals.

If you're looking for another awesome kart racing game, look no further than Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds.

CrossWorlds poses a learning curve that’s oh-so-rewarding to master.

We've spotlighted this deal before, but it's worth repeating for those just seeing this post. This headset is already a steal at its normal price of $27, but for $14, it's virtually irresistible. It's worth a look if you want to level up the audio quality of the games you're playing on Switch 2.

Donkey Kong Bananza is my favorite Switch 2 game, and it's now on sale for $20 off at Amazon! Explore (and destroy) a variety of imaginative worlds as you quest to reach the center of the planet. This package includes the Switch 2 hardware bundled with the flagship launch game, Mario Kart World. It retails for $449, which is $50 off. So if you were still on the fence about getting a Switch 2, this is your chance to save.

Now if you don't like using the stock Joy-Cons on your Nintendo Switch or Switch 2, there are plenty of alternatives. #3184. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments.

#3182. Palmer Luckey says nobody in the West actually wants Ukraine to win

At DealBook, Palmer Luckey said Project Meridian is studying weather control and called for new nuclear tests. He also defended public executions and said he has not let his Facebook firing go.

Anduril founder Palmer Luckey speaks at Space Systems Command, Los Angeles Air Force Base, El Segundo, 6 August 2026

Palmer Luckey says the US government will not let Ukraine use Starshield, because it fears Russia would destroy it. Starshield is the Pentagon’s military satellite network, and SpaceX helps run it. The Anduril founder made the case to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

“The US government isn’t even willing to stand up for Ukraine because they’re afraid of losing their constellation,” Luckey said.

He was defending Elon Musk, who spoke later that day and accused Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield speed limits. Luckey said he likes Musk personally, so people should take his view “with a pound of salt”.

His argument ran like this. Russia has hinted that it could destroy the civilian Starlink network if Ukraine keeps using it for attacks. The same satellites that cover Ukraine also orbit over the US. So Musk should not have to risk his whole network when Washington will not risk its own, Luckey said.

“Nobody in the West actually wants Ukraine to win. They just want them to not lose for as long as possible, which is a bizarre and absurd warfighting position,” he said.

Luckey said he fully supports Ukraine, and that Anduril has worked there since the second day of the war. Who America sells weapons to is not his call, he added.

“I’m a dog on a chain and I need to be kept that way,” Luckey said.

Luckey co-leads Project Meridian, the Pentagon’s 120-day study of future war, with Musk and Newt Gingrich. He said it looks at what war could look like in 2050, and that the MITRE Corporation runs it. The group met at Cheyenne Mountain the day before. It agreed to focus on ideas that have no champion in the Pentagon.

One example is weather control, he said, such as changing where rain falls at sea so forces get a clearer view of targets. He also took credit for pushing the Trump administration to rename the Defense Department the Department of War.

Sorkin read him a criticism from Wes Bryant, who until last year ran the Pentagon’s assessment of civilian harm. Bryant called Meridian a sign of oligarchy in government. Luckey said more than 20 people sit on it, including retired generals and admirals. Nobody attacked Eric Schmidt for joining the Defense Innovation Board under Joe Biden, he said, and the report will be public.

Luckey wants the US to resume nuclear testing, mainly to see what an electromagnetic pulse does to modern electronics. The models used today were built for transistors thousands of times larger than those in a phone, he said. He is not confident his own systems would survive, even when built to the hardening rules.

“They were designed for the type of cell phone that Abraham Lincoln would have used,” he said.

He said no AI model can be controlled, because every major model has been jailbroken within months. Data centres can still be shut off, he added. The AI in weapons is a different technology from chatbots, he argued, and more reliable than the older seekers it replaces.

“I am way more afraid of the civilian collateral side for dumb weapons than I am for smart weapons,” Luckey said.

Some companies have used chatbots for targeting and made mistakes, he said, without naming them. China wants Jensen Huang out of Nvidia, he said, so he wants him back. Luckey still opposes selling chips to China.

Luckey also defended public executions. The state should rarely use the death penalty, he said. When it does, it should do so in public and without medical cover, so people can judge whether it got it right.

“Executions should be brutal. They should be violent,” he said.

He closed on his 2017 firing from Facebook, after he gave $9,000 to a pro-Trump group. He blames former Oculus colleagues, not Mark Zuckerberg, and now works with Meta on a combat headset for the US Army.

“It’s probably better for everybody that I got fired, but I have not let it go,” Luckey said.
